transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-21 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Owen Reed (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (CTO), Priya Kapoor (Lead Engineer), Jamal Thompson (SRE)

Summary (auto-generated, may be fuzzy): Intro walkthrough of Redwood hosted API for chat generation. Discussed streaming behavior and how to set parameters to control randomness and token counts. Walked through retries, exponential backoff, idempotency keys, and console traces. Agreed next steps for sandbox pilot and security docs.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros? I know we're kicking off — we'll run a 30-ish minute demo then leave time for Qs.
[00:15] Carlos (Portbridge CTO): Yeah thanks, we have about 45, so that sounds good. I'm Carlos, CTO. Priya is our lead eng and Jamal handles SRE. Our main ask is: low p95 latency for chat, and predictable costs.
[00:28] Maya: Great. Owen from our infra team will show the sandbox and streaming behavior. Owen?
[00:35] Owen (Redwood SE): Hi all. I'll start with how streaming works on the hosted API, then show param effects and retry patterns. Note: some of the names in the demo are placeholders.
[00:48] Priya (Lead Eng): Quick clarification — when you say streaming, are we getting partial tokens over SSE / websockets? We need to understand how to handle partials and reconnections.
[00:58] Owen: Yes, we stream deltas via SSE by default in our SDKs; you can also use WebSocket where available. Partial chunks come in, the SDK assembles them; if connection drops, you can re-request with since-token or use an idempotency key to resume, but small caveat, resume is best-effort for streamed deltas.
[01:19] Jamal (SRE): Best-effort resume sounds risky. For live chat we can't show gibberish to users during reconnects.
[01:25] Owen: Totally. Common pattern: show partial as 'typing' indicator but buffer until you get a stable sentence boundary. Also we support prefix/KV cache to reduce tokens and keep latency down on repeated contexts.
[01:38] Maya: We'll show an example where caching reduces p95 by about 30ms on repeated prompts.
[01:44] Owen: I'm pulling up the console now — route: /v1/chat, model: redwood-1b-ggml (demo model).
[01:52] [screen share noise]
[02:05] Owen: Here's a simple call: temperature 0.2, top_p 0.9, max_tokens 64. If you lower temperature you reduce randomness; lower top_p trims tail-sampling. For Portbridge, if you want consistent, set temp 0.0–0.3 and keep top_p around 0.8–0.95 depending on your diversity need.
[02:35] Priya: Does that impact latency? If we lower temperature is there any difference CPU-wise?
[02:40] Owen: Not CPU-significant; it's model-internal sampling. The main latency levers are sequence length, kv cache hit rate, batching settings and model size.
[02:51] Carlos: We're also comparing hosted vs dedicated. Our security team prefers dedicated for PII flows. Can we get similar latency on hosted?
[02:59] Maya: Hosted can hit very low latencies especially on smaller models and with prefix caching, but dedicated gives you isolated GPUs and tighter SLOs. There's also private deployment if you need VPC + KMS.
[03:12] Jamal: On encryption — we need KMS integration and customer-managed keys.
[03:17] Maya: Yep, Private supports customer KMS/HSM. For hosted, we offer encryption at rest and in transit and we can present SOC2 docs. I'll attach the security checklist.
[03:28] Owen: Back to retries — pattern we recommend is idempotency key per user-conversation message. For timeout/retry, use exponential backoff with jitter: e.g., initial 200ms, then 500ms, then 1s. Avoid retrying on 4xx.
[03:45] Priya: If a retry happens and the model actually generated but the client didn't receive it, will we get duplicate messages?
[03:52] Owen: That's where idempotency and server-side dedupe helps. If you provide a unique message id, our routing will attempt to detect duplicates for short windows. There's still edge cases with streams where you might get partial + retry; best UX is to confirm final token stream before showing to user.
[04:10] [00:04:12] Maya: We're also happy to enable a small grace period where we persist last response for replay on reconnects during the pilot.
[04:20] Carlos: Nice. Can you show the per-route dashboard? We want to see p50/p95 by model and token cost.
[04:27] Owen: Sure, Console -> Routes -> /v1/chat. You get token breakdowns, average latencies, and trace links to specific requests. We also surface model variant fallbacks if capacity is constrained.
[04:40] [screen: console metrics]
[04:52] Owen: Look here: you can filter by model, by seq length, and see whether KV cache was a hit. That hit-rate column is really useful for cost tuning.
[05:05] Priya: How do we configure batching? Our traffic is steady but with occasional spikes.
[05:10] Owen: Redwood Optimize will recommend batching policies. For hosted you can set continuous batching thresholds, or let the runtime dynamically batch—tradeoff is slightly higher latency for much lower cost. For spikes we recommend burst pools or autoscaling rules (Dedicated offers more control there).
[05:30] Carlos: For our SLA, p95 must be <350ms for short messages (under 50 tokens). Are there published numbers?
[05:38] Maya: We publish benchmark ranges per model in the catalog. For smaller models on hosted in region, p95 for short messages can be ~200–400ms depending on load. We'll share the model profile sheet.
[05:50] Owen: Also, payload shape matters — many tokens up front in system prompts increase latency; we advise trimming user-visible history and using compressed tokens for system instructions when possible.
[06:04] [06:04] Priya: Can you demo a live streaming call and then simulate a dropped connection to show retry UX?
[06:11] Owen: Yep, let's do a live run. I'll start a session, send a 40-token prompt, show the delta stream, then drop the socket.
[06:22] [live demo — auditory typing, brief pause]
[06:32] Owen: Streaming chunk 1: "Sure, here's a quick plan..." chunk 2: "Step one is to..."
[06:42] [simulated disconnect noise]
[06:46] Owen: Now I'll trigger a reconnect from the client with the same idempotency key. You might see a duplicate chunk appear then the SDK trims it because it saw the earlier chunk — that's our dedupe logic.
[07:02] Jamal: There was a moment of glitch where partial sentence showed. In prod we'd like to avoid showing partial sentence fragments.
[07:08] Owen: Agreed — we recommend a tiny buffer on client side (200–400ms) to assemble natural breakpoints. Works well with typing indicator.
[07:18] Maya: For clients where you can't buffer, we can offer server-side truncation to sentence boundaries, but that may add a handful of ms.
[07:27] Priya: On cost — is streaming more expensive than non-streaming?
[07:33] Owen: Token billing is the same; streaming just changes UX. The cost drivers are tokens and model size and number of model calls. Using caching reduces tokens.
[07:43] Carlos: About model fallbacks — if the primary model is busy and you fallback to a smaller variant, is there an API signal so we can log it?
[07:50] Owen: Yes, you get a fallback header in the response and a trace link. The console flags the fallback and shows the variant. You can opt into automatic fallback or manually orchestrate it via routing policies.
[08:03] [08:03] Maya: Let's talk about params briefly — max_tokens caps response length; stop sequences help truncate. Use logprobs sparingly; it increases some compute. Temperature and top_p control sampling. For deterministic transforms use temperature 0 and greedy sampling.
[08:23] Priya: Are there SDKs for our stack? Node + Go + Python?
[08:26] Maya: Yes, all three. We also have a lightweight JS browser SDK that streams over SSE.
[08:33] Jamal: Any caveats with browser streaming and CORS?
[08:36] Owen: CORS headers are set, but we recommend proxying through your backend for auth and to hide keys. For ephemeral clients, use short-lived tokens.
[08:46] Priya: Can we limit token leakage? We need to ensure user data isn't used for model training.
[08:52] Maya: Hosted has a data usage opt-out for customers; Private gives full isolation. We'll attach the data retention & privacy page.
[09:00] Carlos: Security question — does hosted support SSO + RBAC for console?
[09:05] Maya: Yes, SAML SSO with RBAC roles; we also have audit logs per account.
[09:11] Owen: Back to performance — I'll show a quick benchmark: 500 requests, single-threaded, seq len avg 40, model redwood-lite.
[09:20] [benchmark runs; console numbers readout]
[09:30] Owen: p50 120ms, p95 320ms, cache-hit scenario p95 down to 240ms. Your mileage varies with region and concurrent load.
[09:42] Priya: Good numbers. Can we reproduce this in our environment?
[09:46] Owen: We'll provide a reproducible harness you can run against sandbox API key. That will be one of the deliverables.
[09:55] Maya: Quick note on retries and idempotency: make the user-visible message idempotent. If you accept user edits mid-flight you might invalidate the idempotency key.
[10:06] Jamal: For observability, do you integrate with our PagerDuty / Datadog?
[10:10] Maya: Yes, we pipe traces and metrics via OpenTelemetry; Datadog integrations are available and we can send critical alerts to PagerDuty.
[10:18] Carlos: On the pilot — what's a realistic scope? One-week sandbox with 1k synthetic conversations?
[10:23] Owen: Yes, and we'll do two runs: baseline cold cache, and warm cache with prefix caching. We'll measure p50/p95, token counts, and cost delta.
[10:33] Priya: For the sample payloads — are there size limits on system prompts?
[10:37] Owen: There's a practical token limit per model; our console shows sequence length caps. For best perf, trim system prompts and push static instructions to a short tokenized form.
[10:48] [10:48] Maya: I'll follow up with the security checklist and the latency playbook. Owen will attach the benchmark harness and sample requests. Priya, Jamal, you'll get the sandbox key.
[10:58] Priya: Sounds good. One last question — is there a recommended pattern for long-running conversations where KV cache grows?
[11:05] Owen: We recommend summarization of history every N messages to keep seq length small and use external context stores with short pointers. Also TTL on KV cache and per-route cache control.
[11:18] Carlos: Great. Thanks, that was helpful.
[11:22] Maya: Any other questions?
[11:25] Jamal: No, just want to see the logs after benchmark.
[11:28] Maya: We'll send everything. Thanks everyone.
[11:33] [call end]

Post-call notes (auto): Customer is qualified for hosted pilot but may migrate to Dedicated/Private if compliance requires customer-managed KMS. Follow-up items captured in action_items and next_steps above.
questions: How does streaming resume after a disconnect?
What are recommended param ranges for deterministic chat?
How to configure retries and idempotency to avoid duplicates?
Can we get KMS/customer-managed keys for hosted or do we need Private?
